pos: n. (head of a family of the Nethinims who returned from the captivity; written Lebanah in Ezra)
etymology: Hebrew Levana, whiteness, or the moon, from laven, to be white; named once in this spelling, Nehemiah 7:48.
biblical_def: Lebana is the head of one of the Nethinim households in the roll of the return: “The children of Lebana, the children of Hagaba, the children of Shalmai” (Nehemiah 7:48). The Nethinims were the given ones, the temple servants who drew water and cut wood for the house of God, descended in part from the Gibeonites Joshua had bound to that labour. They were the lowest order in the sanctuary's service, and they are listed by household, name after name, for more than twenty verses. Nehemiah explains why he had the register at all: “And my God put into mine heart to gather together the nobles, and the rulers, and the people, that they might be reckoned by genealogy. And I found a register of the genealogy of them which came up at the first” (Nehemiah 7:5). The chapter ends with every rank in its place: “So the priests, and the Levites, and the porters, and the singers, and some of the people, and the Nethinims, and all Israel, dwelt in their cities” (Nehemiah 7:73). Lebana's name means whiteness, and his children are counted in the same document as the priests.

corruption_summary: Menial service is counted as beneath record; the register of the return names the woodcutters and water-drawers household by household.
corruption_paragraphs: An institution that values only its visible offices keeps no roll of its servants. Nehemiah kept one. The Nethinims had no priesthood, no song, no gate to guard, and no inheritance in the land, and they occupy more verses in chapter 7 than the priests do. The list is not condescension; it is a title deed, establishing their right to live in the holy city and serve in the house.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God assigns and honours the lowest station in His house. “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness” (Psalm 84:10). The children of Lebana came up out of Babylon to carry wood, and their father's name is in the word of God.

pos: n. (one of the twelve leaders who came up with Zerubbabel; written Mispar in Ezra)
etymology: Hebrew Misperet, a number, or a writing, from saphar, to count, number or recount; named once in this spelling, Nehemiah 7:7.
biblical_def: Mispereth is one of the twelve men named at the head of the great return: “Who came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, Baanah. The number, I say, of the men of the people of Israel was this” (Nehemiah 7:7). Ezra's parallel list spells the name Mispar, which is how the registers came down. Nothing is told of the man beyond his place in that company, but the place is significant: twelve leaders for twelve tribes, bringing a remnant out of Babylon to a ruined city. His name means a number or a reckoning, and the verse he stands in turns immediately to numbers — the counting of the men of the people of Israel, household by household, through fifty verses. The whole chapter is the work of a man who believed that a people restored by God should be able to say exactly who they were.

corruption_summary: A restored people is imagined as a mood or a movement; Nehemiah restored one by taking a census and writing down the households.
corruption_paragraphs: Renewal is often described in terms that cannot be checked — a spirit, an awakening, a sense of momentum. Nehemiah 7 is almost entirely numbers: seven hundred forty and five of these, three hundred twenty and three of those, the horses, the mules, the camels, the asses, the gold, the basons, the priests' garments. The restoration was countable because it was real.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's work in history takes concrete, documentable form, and that the people of God are a definite people and not an abstraction. The twelve men at the head of the list stand for the twelve tribes, and the fifty verses after them say who actually came.

pos: n. (one of the twelve leaders who came up with Zerubbabel from the captivity)
etymology: Hebrew Nachamani, compassionate, or my comfort, from nacham, to comfort or console; named once, Nehemiah 7:7.
biblical_def: Nahamani stands fifth in the roll of leaders who brought the people home: “Who came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, Baanah” (Nehemiah 7:7). His name is absent from Ezra's parallel list, which is one of the ordinary differences between the two registers, and nothing further is recorded of him. The name itself means comfort, from the root Isaiah uses at the opening of his great consolation. That is the theme of the whole chapter: a register copied out of the early days of the return, found by Nehemiah a lifetime later, proving that God had kept His word to bring a remnant back. The seventh month came and “the children of Israel were in their cities” (Nehemiah 7:73). The comfort promised to Jerusalem was not a feeling but an address.

corruption_summary: Comfort is made an inward state to be cultivated; the comfort God promised Jerusalem was a people brought back to actual houses in actual cities.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic usage has reduced comfort to a feeling managed by technique. The prophets use the word otherwise. When the LORD says comfort ye my people, what follows is a highway, a return, a city rebuilt, and a glory revealed. The consolation of Israel was historical before it was emotional, and the register in Nehemiah 7 is part of the proof.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the comfort of God comes to His people in deeds, and the deeds can be dated and counted. A man named my comfort walked back from Babylon at the head of a column, and the chapter he is in ends with Israel in their cities on the first day of the seventh month, at which point Ezra opened the book.

pos: n. (one of the chief of the people who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah)
etymology: Hebrew Magpi'ash, of uncertain derivation, taken by some as collector of a cluster or moth-killer; named once, Nehemiah 10:20.
biblical_def: Magpiash is a name on a legal document. Nehemiah 10 lists those who set their seal to the covenant Israel made after the law had been read and the people had wept: “Magpiash, Meshullam, Hezir” (Nehemiah 10:20). The signatories begin with the governor — “Now those that sealed were, Nehemiah, the Tirshatha, the son of Hachaliah, and Zidkijah” (Nehemiah 10:1) — and run through the priests, the Levites, and the chief of the people, of whom Magpiash is one. The substance of what they signed is given plainly: the rest of the people “clave to their brethren, their nobles, and entered into a curse, and into an oath, to walk in God's law, which was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the LORD our Lord, and his judgments and his statutes” (Nehemiah 10:29). They bound themselves under a curse. The terms that follow are specific: no marriages with the people of the land, no trading on the sabbath, the seventh year release, a wood offering, the firstfruits, the tithes, and the standing resolution, “we will not forsake the house of our God” (Nehemiah 10:39).

corruption_summary: Commitment is kept deliberately vague so that nothing can be breached; Nehemiah's generation wrote theirs down, named the terms, sealed it, and took a curse upon themselves.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern religious resolve avoids specificity. Vows are thought legalistic, written commitments rigid, and naming the particular sins to be forsaken is felt to be harsh. Nehemiah 10 is the opposite in every respect. The people identified the exact practices that had destroyed them — intermarriage with the nations, sabbath-breaking commerce, neglect of the house of God — and bound themselves by oath, in writing, with their names attached.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is covenanting: the public, specific, sworn binding of a people to God's law. It is the instinct behind every Reformed confession and every church covenant that followed. Magpiash is one of eighty-four men who understood that a resolution nobody signs is a resolution nobody keeps.

pos: n. (the second name on the sealed covenant of Nehemiah 10, after the Tirshatha)
etymology: Hebrew Tsidqiyyah, the LORD is righteousness, from tsedeq, righteousness, with Yah; the same name borne by king Zedekiah, here in the Authorized Version's alternate English form; named once, Nehemiah 10:1.
biblical_def: Zidkijah signs second: “Now those that sealed were, Nehemiah, the Tirshatha, the son of Hachaliah, and Zidkijah” (Nehemiah 10:1). After him come the priests, then the Levites, then the chief of the people. Who he was is not said — possibly the governor's secretary, possibly a leading priest — but the position of his name next to Nehemiah's is itself a statement about how the covenant was made. It began at the top. The Tirshatha did not require of the people what he would not sign first, and the document ran downward from him through every order in the nation to the women and the children old enough to understand: “And the rest of the people, the priests, the Levites, the porters, the singers, the Nethinims, and all they that had separated themselves from the people of the lands unto the law of God, their wives, their sons, and their daughters, every one having knowledge, and having understanding” (Nehemiah 10:28). His name means the LORD is righteousness, which is the ground on which any such covenant can be kept at all.

corruption_summary: Leaders exempt themselves from the standard they set; the covenant of Nehemiah 10 was signed by the governor first and the people afterward.
corruption_paragraphs: A reform imposed downward and evaded upward is not a reform. Nehemiah's name heads the document, Zidkijah's follows it, and the priests and Levites come next, before a single name of the people appears. The chapter before states the resolution: “And because of all this we make a sure covenant, and write it; and our princes, Levites, and priests, seal unto it” (Nehemiah 9:38). The princes sealed first.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that lawful authority binds itself before it binds others. Elders who require of a congregation what they will not themselves profess have no standing to require it. The Hebrew in this man's name is the only guarantee the arrangement ever had: the LORD is righteousness, and therefore a sworn people may hope to keep their oath.

pos: n. (the Gibeonite who repaired a portion of the wall of Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Melatyah, the LORD hath delivered, from malat, to escape or be delivered, with Yah; named once, Nehemiah 3:7.
biblical_def: Melatiah is one of the builders, and his designation matters: “And next unto them repaired Melatiah the Gibeonite, and Jadon the Meronothite, the men of Gibeon, and of Mizpah, unto the throne of the governor on this side the river” (Nehemiah 3:7). A Gibeonite was a descendant of the men who deceived Joshua with mouldy bread and worn shoes, and who were spared under oath but condemned to be hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of God. Centuries later their children are rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem with their own names recorded beside the goldsmiths and the apothecaries. The section they took ran up to the seat of the Persian governor, a conspicuous and exposed stretch. Nehemiah's chapter credits every party by name and neighbour — “And between the going up of the corner unto the sheep gate repaired the goldsmiths and the merchants” (Nehemiah 3:32) — and in that list a Gibeonite stands as a builder of the holy city. His name means the LORD hath delivered.

corruption_summary: A people's origin is treated as their ceiling; the descendants of Joshua's deceivers are named among the builders of Jerusalem's wall.
corruption_paragraphs: Where a group has a disgraceful beginning, the assumption is that it carries the stain permanently, or else that the stain must be denied. Scripture does neither. Joshua 9 is kept on record: the Gibeonites lied, the oath was sworn, and Joshua “made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD” (Joshua 9:27). Nehemiah 3 is also kept on record, and in it a Gibeonite builds.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God brings strangers into the service of His house without pretending they were never strangers. The sentence passed on Gibeon was service at the altar, and service at the altar is where their children ended up, by mercy rather than by right. “So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work” (Nehemiah 4:6).

pos: n. (the Meronothite who repaired a portion of the wall of Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Yadon, he will judge, or thankful, from din, to judge or contend; named once, Nehemiah 3:7.
biblical_def: Jadon works beside Melatiah in the same clause: “And next unto them repaired Melatiah the Gibeonite, and Jadon the Meronothite, the men of Gibeon, and of Mizpah, unto the throne of the governor on this side the river” (Nehemiah 3:7). He is the second of only two men in Scripture called Meronothite, the other being an officer of David five centuries earlier, and his town is nowhere described. What is clear is the shape of the work: men came in from the outlying towns — Jericho, Tekoa, Gibeon, Mizpah, Zanoah, Beth-haccerem — to repair a wall that was not their own, in a city most of them did not live in. The section Jadon and his neighbours took ran to the seat of the Persian governor. Nehemiah built under open hostility, and the chapter after this one records the answer: “every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon” (Nehemiah 4:17). Jadon is one of the men holding both.

corruption_paragraphs: The modern calculation asks what a man gets from the work before he gives himself to it. Nehemiah 3 lists builders from Jericho, Tekoa, Gibeon, Mizpah, Zanoah and Beth-zur, none of whom would sleep inside the wall they raised. They came because Jerusalem was the city of the great King and its ruin was Israel's shame, not because the benefit fell to them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is a love for the house and city of God that is not calculated by private advantage. “So the wall was finished in the twenty and fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty and two days” (Nehemiah 6:15). That is what fifty-two days of men like Jadon produced, with a trowel in one hand and a sword in the other.

pos: n. (the father of Hanun, who repaired another piece of the wall of Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Tsalaph, fracture, or wounded, of uncertain root; named once, Nehemiah 3:30.
biblical_def: Zalaph is named only as a father, and the detail given about his family is unusually specific: “After him repaired Hananiah the son of Shelemiah, and Hanun the sixth son of Zalaph, another piece. After him repaired Meshullam the son of Berechiah over against his chamber” (Nehemiah 3:30). The sixth son. Nehemiah had no administrative need to record the birth order of a builder, and the fact that he did is characteristic of the whole chapter, which notices that Shallum's daughters worked, that Baruch repaired earnestly, that Meshullam built opposite his own chamber, and that the Tekoite nobles “put not their necks to the work of their Lord” (Nehemiah 3:5). The register is a moral record as much as a construction log. Hanun took on another piece, a second stretch beyond his first, and he did it as the sixth son of a man otherwise unknown. The name Zalaph means a fracture, and his son was mending one.

corruption_summary: Work records note output; Nehemiah's notes who held back, who did a second portion, and whose daughters laboured beside him.
corruption_paragraphs: A list of contractors is normally neutral. Nehemiah 3 is not. It records that the nobles of Tekoa “put not their necks to the work of their Lord” (Nehemiah 3:5) while their townsmen built two separate sections; that Shallum repaired “he and his daughters” (Nehemiah 3:12); that Baruch the son of Zabbai “earnestly repaired the other piece” (Nehemiah 3:20). The Holy Ghost saw fit to preserve both the diligence and the refusal.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God observes the manner of our work and not merely its completion. Hanun the sixth son of Zalaph took another piece when he had already done one. The men of Tekoa whose nobles would not stoop are named twice as builders. Nothing done or withheld in the work of God goes unrecorded.

pos: n. (a priest of the house of Moadiah in the days of Joiakim)
etymology: Hebrew Piltay, my deliverances, or the LORD delivers, from palat, to escape or deliver; named once, Nehemiah 12:17.
biblical_def: Piltai belongs to a chapter of priestly succession: “Of Abijah, Zichri; of Miniamin, of Moadiah, Piltai” (Nehemiah 12:17). The list records which man was the chief of the fathers for each priestly house in the days of Joiakim, the son of Jeshua the high priest — the second generation after the return. The chapter opens with the priests who came up with Zerubbabel (Nehemiah 12:1) and then gives their successors: “And in the days of Joiakim were priests, the chief of the fathers: of Seraiah, Meraiah; of Jeremiah, Hananiah” (Nehemiah 12:12). It is a handover list. The men who crossed the desert out of Babylon had died or grown old, and the record shows who took up each course after them. A restored church lasts only as long as the second generation is identified, trained and installed, and Nehemiah wrote the names down.

corruption_summary: Succession is treated as institutional inertia; in a restored church it is the difference between a revival and a generation.
corruption_paragraphs: Attention goes to founders. The men who came up with Zerubbabel have their chapter, and so they should; but Nehemiah 12 spends its second half on who followed them, course by course, house by house. Without that list the restoration would have been a single generation's achievement and would have died with them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the deliberate handing on of ministry. “And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). Piltai's whole recorded life is that he was the man of Moadiah's house in the next generation, and that was enough to be written down.

pos: n. (one of the sons of Bani who had taken a strange wife in Ezra's day)
etymology: Hebrew Maknadvay, of uncertain derivation, perhaps gift of the noble one; the Authorized Version's margin notes that some copies read Mabnadebai; named once, Ezra 10:40.
biblical_def: Machnadebai stands near the end of the hardest list in Ezra: the names of the men who had married wives from the peoples of the land and who put them away. “Machnadebai, Shashai, Sharai” (Ezra 10:40) comes in the long roll of the sons of Bani, and the chapter closes with the flat summary, “All these had taken strange wives: and some of them had wives by whom they had children” (Ezra 10:44). The crisis was not racial but covenantal: Israel had been commanded not to bind itself in marriage to nations whose gods it would then serve, and the returned remnant had begun doing precisely what had destroyed the first commonwealth. Ezra's response was to sit astonied until the evening sacrifice, to tear his garment and pluck out his hair, and then to confess the sin as his own. The men are named because they repented publicly, and a public sin requires a public remedy. There is no softening of the register and no anonymity in it.

corruption_summary: Naming those who sinned is read as shaming; Ezra 10 names them because the sin was public, the remedy was public, and the record is their repentance.
corruption_paragraphs: A list of offenders offends modern sensibility, which prefers that wrongdoing be handled privately and that no name be attached. Ezra 10 attaches more than a hundred. But the chapter is not a pillory. These are the men who came, confessed, gave their hands, and did the costly thing; the register is the record of their obedience, and the only men in Ezra's day who escape being named are the ones who refused to come.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that public sin calls for public repentance, and that the church's record of such repentance is a mercy and not a brand. Ezra's charge was plain: “Now therefore make confession unto the LORD God of your fathers, and do his pleasure: and separate yourselves from the people of the land, and from the strange wives” (Ezra 10:11). Machnadebai did.
